title: Chapter 64 — Account Rescue
intro: Recovering accounts after a service failure, delivery disaster, or relationship breakdown.

sections.title: Diagnosing the Damage
sections.content:
An account in trouble shows warning signs before it dies: fewer quote requests, longer response times, projects going to competitors, and reduced communication. By the time you notice, the builder has already started shifting volume.

Diagnose the root cause honestly. Was it a delivery failure? A pricing dispute? A missed spec that caused a job site problem? An unresponsive follow-up? You cannot rescue what you do not understand.

Call the decision maker directly. 'I have noticed we have not worked together in a while. I want to understand what happened and what I can do to earn your business back. Can I buy you a coffee?'

sections.title: The Rescue Conversation
sections.content:
Listen without defending. If they say 'your delivery was late on the Morrison project and it cost me a day of labour,' do not explain why. Say 'You are right. That should not have happened. Here is what we have changed since then.' Then show them the specific operational change you made.

Offer a concrete gesture: 'I would like to earn a second chance. Let me quote your next project — if the delivery is not perfect, I will personally cover the re-delivery cost.' Put skin in the game. The builder who sees you accept risk is more likely to give you the opportunity.

sections.title: Rebuilding Trust
sections.content:
The rescue is not a single conversation. It is a campaign. Quote the next project aggressively. Deliver flawlessly. Follow up proactively. Send the post-delivery confirmation before they ask.

Over-deliver on the first 2-3 rescue projects. Set expectations low and exceed them. The account that was rescued often becomes more loyal than one that was never at risk — because you proved you would fight for the relationship.
